Despite the growing body of research, there is a lack of understanding of how to effectively apply these representations to classify graphs. 
This paper aims to address this gap by examining the relationship between graph structure and the ability of node representations to be distinguished. 
We introduce a novel approach that leverages the concept of the "independence of node representations," measured by the mutual information between these representations and the graph. 
Our method, Mutual Information Graph Embedding (MIGE), uses a mutual information-based loss function to optimize graph representations. 
We demonstrate the effectiveness of MIE through theoretical analysis and experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets, showcasing its superiority over state-of-the-art graph embedding methods. 
Our results also reveal the limitations of traditional loss functions used in graph embedding, such as contrastive loss. 
This work provides a new perspective on the relationship between graph structure and the ability of node representations to be distinguished, as well as a new approach to learning effective graph representations. 
The code for MIGE is available at https://github.com/WeihongShen/MIGE.
